According to are we saying that converting ETH to USD first and then USD to USDC would result a correct value of ETH in USDC while converting ETH to USDC directly would result an incorrect value of ETH in USDC?

submission_issue_comments.author: pkqs90
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @gzeon-c4, despite this being a creative attack, the contest README clearly states that keepers are trusted.

 

Only the keeper contract is allowed to make calls to balancer flashloan: 

According to this should fall under admin mistakes and considered a centralization risk, which is QA/low severity.

submission_issue_comments.author: alexxander77
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @pkqs90, 

Every Vault has its own separate Keeper (keeperContract). While it is true that users should trust the Keeper of the Vault they deposit into, it is unreasonable to expect them to trust the Keepers of other Vaults. The distinction here is that users entrust their funds to the Keeper of their specific Vault, not to the Keepers of other Vaults.

In the broader context of the Noya contracts, there are many strategy managers with their own Keepers and Vaults, potentially competing against each other. The ability of a Vault’s Keeper to access and exploit another Vault’s funds is a significant risk, not merely a QA/low severity issue.

submission_issue_comments.author: pkqs90
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @alexxander77, I see what you're saying. However, I have some questions:

1) Where does the different vaults are potentially competing against each other come from? From it only says multiple vaults are created for specified intent and security settings.

2) From public information (readme, docs), it is understood that vaults are handled by keepers/strategy managers which are handled by the admin team (which is trusted as stated by the readme), in what scenario would the admin apply a strategy to pull funds from other vaults?

3) My understanding of the trusted keyword used in readme is that the trusted roles would not do evil or make mistakes to harm users. It says that the keepers role is trusted, which I think it should be assumed that keepers role should be trusted by all users, instead of being only trusted by users of its own vault.

submission_issue_comments.author: alexxander77
submission_issue_comments.body:
In this situation, interpreting and relying solely on the trusted roles table is challenging. From the point of view of users, a Keeper of a Vault should be trusted. From the point of view of Keeper to Keeper and Maintainer to Keeper it is not obvious and more nuanced. By default, a newly added Vault with a Keeper shouldn't have any power over other Keeper's Vaults and their funds (code link), which shows a degree of trust between a Maintainer and a Keeper that is completely different compared to if the Maintainer knows that a Keeper can exploit any other Keeper of their funds. My personal interpretation of the current trust assumptions is that a Keeper must not be able to exploit other Keepers. 

The code in the modifier NoyaGovernanceBase.onlyManager() (code link), along with the access control check in BalancerFlashLoan.receiveFlashLoan()(code link), clearly shows there is an access control mechanism employed that is supposed to allow only the Keeper of a Vault to interact with that Vault. The submission demonstrates that this assumption does not hold true and leads to a theft of funds. Nonetheless, thanks for the input, @pkqs90.

submission_issue_comments.author: jorgect207

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @gzeon-c4, despite this being a creative attack, the contest README clearly states that keepers are trusted.

 

Only the keeper contract is allowed to make calls to balancer flashloan: 

According to this should fall under admin mistakes and considered a centralization risk, which is QA/low severity.

submission_issue_comments.author: alexxander77
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @pkqs90, 

Every Vault has its own separate Keeper (keeperContract). While it is true that users should trust the Keeper of the Vault they deposit into, it is unreasonable to expect them to trust the Keepers of other Vaults. The distinction here is that users entrust their funds to the Keeper of their specific Vault, not to the Keepers of other Vaults.

In the broader context of the Noya contracts, there are many strategy managers with their own Keepers and Vaults, potentially competing against each other. The ability of a Vault’s Keeper to access and exploit another Vault’s funds is a significant risk, not merely a QA/low severity issue.

submission_issue_comments.author: pkqs90
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @alexxander77, I see what you're saying. However, I have some questions:

1) Where does the different vaults are potentially competing against each other come from? From it only says multiple vaults are created for specified intent and security settings.

2) From public information (readme, docs), it is understood that vaults are handled by keepers/strategy managers which are handled by the admin team (which is trusted as stated by the readme), in what scenario would the admin apply a strategy to pull funds from other vaults?

3) My understanding of the trusted keyword used in readme is that the trusted roles would not do evil or make mistakes to harm users. It says that the keepers role is trusted, which I think it should be assumed that keepers role should be trusted by all users, instead of being only trusted by users of its own vault.

submission_issue_comments.author: alexxander77
submission_issue_comments.body:
In this situation, interpreting and relying solely on the trusted roles table is challenging. From the point of view of users, a Keeper of a Vault should be trusted. From the point of view of Keeper to Keeper and Maintainer to Keeper it is not obvious and more nuanced. By default, a newly added Vault with a Keeper shouldn't have any power over other Keeper's Vaults and their funds (code link), which shows a degree of trust between a Maintainer and a Keeper that is completely different compared to if the Maintainer knows that a Keeper can exploit any other Keeper of their funds. My personal interpretation of the current trust assumptions is that a Keeper must not be able to exploit other Keepers. 

The code in the modifier NoyaGovernanceBase.onlyManager() (code link), along with the access control check in BalancerFlashLoan.receiveFlashLoan()(code link), clearly shows there is an access control mechanism employed that is supposed to allow only the Keeper of a Vault to interact with that Vault. The submission demonstrates that this assumption does not hold true and leads to a theft of funds. Nonetheless, thanks for the input, @pkqs90.

submission_issue_comments.author: HadiEsna
submission_issue_comments.body:
The reason of dividing by weight is to get the total value of the vault.
So it can work on both stable and weighted vaults
imagine there is a vault with 3 tokens with 100$ worth of tokens in each reserve
When we get the total amount of the tokens we get 100$ and we want to know how much in total we own from the vault
So we divide this 100 by its weight and multiply by the sum of weights (here is 100/13) which will give us 300$

submission_issue_comments.author: HadiEsna
submission_issue_comments.body:
The reason of dividing by weight is to get the total value of the vault.
So it can work on both stable and weighted vaults
imagine there is a vault with 3 tokens with 100$ worth of tokens in each reserve
When we get the total amount of the tokens we get 100$ and we want to know how much in total we own from the vault
So we divide this 100 by its weight and multiply by the sum of weights (here is 100/13) which will give us 300$

submission_issue_comments.author: yotov721
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi, On the comment that @jorgect207 left:
1. Yes, that is correct - it can be called only by the manager.
2. NOYA and Silo have different health factor tolerance. For NOYA it is 150% collateralization and for other protocols it is lower - 120% for example. This way NOYA adds a buffer on top of the protocol's min Liquidation ration.
NOYA has set the default value to 1.5e18 in the base connector. Having in mind that 1e18 is 100 %. 
The calculation is ok for most protocols, but in the case with Silo it is calculated a different way. That is why NOYA have added the SolvencyV2 contract and buffed up the minimumHealthFactor adding a buffer. 

Having all this in mind, the borrow is only protected by the CR of the Silo protocol and not taking into account NOYA's buffer. Hence NOYA manager can mint position bellow NOYA's desired CR and then can not repay it partialy because of the check in deposit().

submission_issue_comments.author: yotov721
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi, On the comment that @jorgect207 left:
1. Yes, that is correct - it can be called only by the manager.
2. NOYA and Silo have different health factor tolerance. For NOYA it is 150% collateralization and for other protocols it is lower - 120% for example. This way NOYA adds a buffer on top of the protocol's min Liquidation ration.
NOYA has set the default value to 1.5e18 in the base connector. Having in mind that 1e18 is 100 %. 
The calculation is ok for most protocols, but in the case with Silo it is calculated a different way. That is why NOYA have added the SolvencyV2 contract and buffed up the minimumHealthFactor adding a buffer. 

Having all this in mind, the borrow is only protected by the CR of the Silo protocol and not taking into account NOYA's buffer. Hence NOYA manager can mint position bellow NOYA's desired CR and then can not repay it partialy because of the check in deposit().

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xAlix2
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hello @gzeon-c4, thanks for judging this!

I'm afraid I have to disagree with this resolution, I don't think this is a duplicate of #862, where that only introduces an enhancement to comply with the "naming" of it. Where this issue shows that the protocol incorrectly handles the holding position of the connector, in the attached POC, the user moved funds from an account to another and the TVL is dropped to 0, as the new account's position is not added as a holding position. The connector has to explicitly add/remove an account's holding positions according to the opened markets.

As a result, this should be a high separate issue (looking into how you folks are dealing with similar TVL issues).

Thanks!

submission_issue_comments.author: mcgrathcoutinho
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @gzeon-c4, I believe this issue should of valid Medium-severity.

MaverickConnector being able to earn staking reward is not a defined behavior.

It is a defined behaviour since the MaverickConnector implements a function to claim boosted position rewards. But due to it's incorrect implementation it is not able to do so. If it wasn't the expected behaviour, I do not think the sponsor would have confirmed the issue.

I think this should be a valid Medium-severity issue considering how other issues describing lack of reward/fees claiming functionality or loss of yield/incentives have been judged, which ends up with protocol not receiving their deserved rewards. At the end, the main reason connectors are used is to increase the TVL of the Noya protocol, which the Maverick Connector fails to do (i.e. expected functionality of the contract is impacted and unavailable). 

Please consider re-evaluating this issue.

Thank you for your time!

submission_issue_comments.author: mcgrathcoutinho
submission_issue_comments.body:
@gzeoneth Just want to clarify, I do not think this is a dup of #1100 since here the functionality itself is affected i.e. boosted position rewards "cannot be collected" through function claimBoostedPositionRewards() in the first place due to the incorrect implementation while in #1100 it is just saying that the fees/yield which "are collected" are not realtime when reporting TVL.

Similar issues like #976 and #712 have been judged as medium.

patch.explanation: Check for these extra reward tokens and updated them in the registry using the updateTokenInRegistry function.

poc.reproducibility_note: PoC code is quoted from the published report and was not executed during dataset construction. Running it requires the audited repository at the recorded commit plus the audit's own test harness, neither of which is vendored here.
poc.setup: In the `harvestConvexRewards` function - ```solidity function harvestConvexRewards(address[] calldata rewardsPools) public onlyManager nonReentrant { for (uint256 i = 0; i < rewardsPools.length; i++) { IConvexBasicRewards baseRewardPool = IConvexBasicRewards(rewardsPools[i]); baseRewardPool.getReward(address(this), true); } _updateTokenInRegistry(CVX); _updateTokenInRegistry(CRV); emit HarvestConvexRewards(rewardsPools); } ``` Only CVX and CRV tokens are updated. But, when `baseRewardPool.getReward(address(this), true);` is called, the connector can also receive extra rewards.

submission_issue_comments.author: d3e4
submission_issue_comments.body:
The argument for invalidating this applies only to the impact of losing the fees. The fees are indeed not permanently lost after a single attack. What is at stake here is rather a DoS of fee collection. The previous impact seems High, but the latter is still at the Medium level (especially since it is very likely and trivial to execute).
It is a clear bug which is easy to fix.

submission_issue_comments.author: gzeon-c4
submission_issue_comments.body: I don't think we should assume the tvl is easily manipulatable without cost. Given the manipulation cost and the eventual correctness, I think the risk is low here. The fact that this is acknoledged in a previous audit ( also make it out-of-scope.

submission_issue_comments.author: d3e4
submission_issue_comments.body:
@gzeon-c4 It is a matter of 1 wei. I think any update to the tvl will be a decrease with around 50% probability (any random noise would suffice). And if manipulatable, it should not cost anything but dust and gas fees to manipulate by 1 wei.

What was acknowledged before was the risk of losing the fees altogether. But it is the DoS that should be considered here.

patch.explanation: The AccountingManager contract can be updated to add the maxDeposit, maxMint, maxWithdraw, and maxRedeem functions to override the corresponding functions in OpenZeppelin's ERC4626 contract. To be compliant with the EIP-4626 standard, these functions can always return 0 since calling the deposit(uint256 assets, address receiver), mint(uint256 shares, address receiver), withdraw(uint256 assets, address receiver, address owner), and redeem(uint256 shares, address receiver, address shareOwner) functions always revert. Moreover, two more functions that are similar to the maxDeposit and maxRedeem functions can be added in the AccountingManager contract to accompany the deposit(address receiver, uint256 amount, address referrer) and withdraw(uint256 share, address receiver) functions, and these two additional functions should respectively return 0 when the corresponding deposit and withdraw functions are respectively paused.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hello @gzeon-c4,

I believe the issues grouped as duplicates of this one are not entirely the same. Some of them mention only one specific problem, which is that the data parameter is not hashed with keccak256. These issues include: #37, #82, #274, #942, #870, #1065, #871, #869, #560, #257, #1453, #1354, and #1252.

Others point out a different problem, which is that the typeHash has an incorrect trailing space. These issues include: #51 and #459.

Because of these distinctions, I think they are only partially addressing the issue. Therefore, they should be grouped separately or marked as partial duplicates.

patch.explanation: When calculating the TVL of a position held by the BalancerConnector, make sure to include the unclaimed rewards. attack_path.action: In the Balancer protocol, users can earn rewards by depositing their LP tokens in the AuraPool.
The calculated TVL of a vault is the basis to determine how much value a user gets when withdrawing shares from the vault.
if a user redeems 10% of all vault shares he will get 10% of the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, any user who withdraws from the vault will receive less value for his shares than he should be receiving.

The calculated TVL is also used to determine how many shares a user gets when depositing to the vault by multiplying the value the user wants to supply with the outstanding shares and dividing it by the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, users depositing to the vault will get more share minted to them than they should be getting.

submission_issue_comments.author: BenRai1
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @DadeKuma,
as far as I know V3 of the pendle protocol is not yet out. You can see this by clicking at the three dots in the right top corner on the current website. There is a link to the V1 App but not to a V2 suggesting the current app is V2. I would say NOYA is using V2 and not V1 since V1 it is no longer active. Since the current version of the Protocol is V2, when referring to the current version in the issue description, I am talking about V2 (sorry for not making this totally clear).
As stated in Pendle’s official FAQ, one does not need to stake the LP to get rewards. Therefore, as described in the issue above, the calculation of the TVL will be DOSed and therefore the issue should be a valid high.

submission_issue_comments.author: BenRai1
submission_issue_comments.body: Thanks for the links. I contacted the pendler team about this and now everything makes sence. According to the team, the router version is irelevant for staking LP tokens, only thing relevant is the Pendler version. The current version is V2 and "since day 1 of Pendle V2" there is no need to stake the LP tokens. This should mean that issue is valid since NOYA will interact with the current version of Pendle which is V2. Sorry for the confusing responce above with the different versions, had some trouble remembering the exact sircumstances. The link to the conversation on the Pendle Discord is here

submission_issue_comments.author: BenRai1
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @HadiEsna,
some more info about my approach to test this issue. I used the PendleMarketDepositHelper on Etherium and one of the currently active markets/pools, namely the ankrETH-wstETH Pool with the market address 0xd547d9c74314f787affc587d101146e1663d046e. (click on Info on the pool site to find the address)

If you try to call balance on Etherscan with the market address 0xd547d9c74314f787affc587d101146e1663d046e and any user address, the call reverts. 

This makes sense since the code for balance(), which you are also calling when calculating the TVL for the pendle connector (pendleMarketDepositHelper.balance(market, address(this))) is the following:

 [code] 
The rewarder for new pools in V2 within the poolInfo mapping is not set because since V2 restaking of LP tokens is not required any more. This means that the returned rewarder is address(0) and if you call address(0) with any function call it will revert since the address does not hold any code. 
Can you share which addresses you used for your test? (address of the market and address of the MarketDepositHelper).
If you test it with an old pool/market which was already supported in PendleV1, the call will not revert since a rewarder has been set for it in the past.

patch.explanation: When fraxlendPair.maxLTV = 0, FraxConnector.getHealthFactor() should return type(uint256).max.

poc.reproducibility_note: PoC code is quoted from the published report and was not executed during dataset construction. Running it requires the audited repository at the recorded commit plus the audit's own test harness, neither of which is vendored here.
poc.setup: `FraxConnector._getHealthFactor()` returns 0 when the `_fraxlendPair.maxLTV = 0`. ```solidity FraxConnector.sol 132: uint256 fraxlendPairMaxLTV = _fraxlendPair.maxLTV(); 133: if (currentPositionLTV == 0) return type(uint256).max; // loan is small 134: 135: // // convert LTVs to HF 136: uint256 currentHF = ( fraxlendPairMaxLTV * 1e18) / currentPositionLTV; ``` But as we can see from the implementation of `FraxlendPairCore.sol`, when `maxLTV` is set to 0, the fraxlend pair is always solvent so we can think that the maximum LTV is infinity instead of 0.

submission_issue_comments.author: KupiaSecAdmin
submission_issue_comments.body: Inside Fraxlend protocol, as we can see from the implementation of FraxlendPairCore.sol, when maxLTV is 0, the fraxlend pair is always solvent so we can think that the actual value of maximum LTV is infinity instead of 0. And this affects the calculation of currentHF here. When fraxlendPair.maxLTV = 0, the health factor of FraxConnector should be type(uint256).max instead of 0. And borrowAndSupply() and withdraw() of FraxConnector should not be blocked in this case.

patch.explanation:
When calculating the TVL of a position held by the SNXV3Connector, make sure to include the unclaimed rewards. This can be done by calling SNXCoreProxy.getAvailableRewards().
Determine the value of the rewards by calling getValue for the reward token and add the value to the returned TVL of the position.

attack_path.action: In the Syntetix protocol, users can earn rewards by maintain a target collateral ratio / health factor.
The calculated TVL of a vault is the basis to determine how much value a user gets when withdrawing shares from the vault.
if a user redeems 10% of all vault shares he will get 10% of the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, any user who withdraws from the vault will receive less value for his shares than he should be receiving.

The calculated TVL is also used to determine how many shares a user gets when depositing to the vault by multiplying the value the user wants to supply with the outstanding shares and dividing it by the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, users depositing to the vault will get more share minted to them than they should be getting.

submission_issue_comments.author: iamandreiski
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi, thanks for judging and for the very prompt turnaround on the whole process. 

Regarding this particular issue, I believe that it is wrongly dupped. It isn’t related to balance changes outside of transfers, rather it’s the inability of the NoyaFeeReceiver to handle fees in the form of ERC20 tokens, i.e. the contract’s lack of logic/functions that handles ERC20 tokens, while the withdraw fee mechanics utilizes ERC20 tokens.

As outlined above, multiple deployed instances of the NoyaFeeReceiver contract will collect different fees ,e.g. performance fee or as the case outlined above - withdraw fee. The problem is that all fees are usually minted as shares to the NoyaFeeReceiver (as they should), but in the case above (withdraw fee transferred to an instance of the NoyaFeeReceiver dedicated solely to the withdraw fee collection), but the withdraw fees are not minted as shares but rather sent to the contract directly. Since the contract logic can’t handle ERC20 tokens, the fees sent to it will be lost.

The NoyaFeeReceiver needs to implement ERC20-funtions related logic so that it can transfer/use the withdraw fees.

attack_path.action: The calculated TVL of a vault is the basis to determine how much value a user gets when withdrawing shares from the vault.
if a user redeems 10% of all vault shares he will get 10% of the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL of the vault is lower than the actual vault TVL, any user who withdraws from the vault will receive less value for his shares than he should be receiving.
The calculated vault TVL is also used to determine how many shares a user gets when depositing to the vault.
This is done by multiplying the value the user wants to supply with the outstanding shares of the vault and dividing it by the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, users depositing to the vault will get more share minted to them than they should be getting.

attack_path.action: The calculated TVL of a vault is the basis to determine how much value a user gets when withdrawing shares from the vault.
if a user redeems 10% of all vault shares he will get 10% of the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL of the vault is lower than the actual vault TVL, any user who withdraws from the vault will receive less value for his shares than he should be receiving.
The calculated vault TVL is also used to determine how many shares a user gets when depositing to the vault.
This is done by multiplying the value the user wants to supply with the outstanding shares of the vault and dividing it by the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, users depositing to the vault will get more share minted to them than they should be getting.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @gzeon-c4,
I agree that manager is a trusted role, but in the PoC(attack vector) the malicious user calls MorphoBlue::repay() directly, with onBehalf the NOYA connector's address. The attacker does not call MorphoBlueConnector::repay() which is callable only be the manager. MorphoBlue::repay() is a function of Mopho Blue, not NOYA - it is called by MorphoBlueConnector::repay().

I've added some comments to the PoC:
 [code] 

The problem is that an attacker can prevent NOYA from repaying its debt in MorphoBlue. 
We believe the issue is valid one for the following reasons:
- Since NOYA works with many types of assets, this implies that some of them will have higher volatility than others. In these situations it is imperative to have DoS-proof functions in the contracts, since delays can cause protocol loss. 
- When building DeFi integration contracts it is important to comply with the mechanics of said DeFi protocols. Because MorphoBlue allows debt repayment by anyone and over-repaying will revert - this is something that a connector contract should take into account.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey, how's it going?

Issues #830 and #831 are duplicates of one another, and issue #824 is a separate finding. Those issues are not duplicates of #991.
Here's my reasoning:
 According to C4 documentation:
Findings are duplicates if they share the same root cause.

More specifically, if fixing the Root Cause (in a reasonable manner) would cause the finding to no longer be exploitable, then the findings are duplicates.


For the issues mentioned, fixing one issue does not fix the other at all. If it wasn't reported, the protocol would be left exposed to slippage on other parts of its connectors. Duplicating the issues with the lack of slippage control with other protocol integrations is misleading as the sponsor may end up believing the issue is a single one and fix one part of the codebase while leaving many other parts exposed. 

 
 Acknowledging no slippage control at the protocol as a single root cause is a false premise. 
The protocol does know about slippage and also implements protection on some of its connectors. 
Examples: 
The UNIV3Connector within its usage of the MintParams struct at at and at .

The BaseConnector acknowledges slippage checks on its dev comments: 

 Issue #1018 is a different Pendle slippage issue that is not a duplicate of #991.
Issues 830 and 831 are relative to MorphoConnector slippage, 824 is relative to Aave slippage and neither have been submitted elsewhere.

Thanks for your time!

submission_issue_comments.author: iamandreiski
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi, thanks again for your judging efforts, I believe the primary issue doesn’t paint the whole picture around the problem that’s why I’m commenting on this one. 

I believe this should be a valid issue since the problem with Dolomite isn’t a simple health factor check as with other connectors, here the problem is two-fold:

- The Dolomite position(s) can be put in a borrowing state without actually opening a borrow position, but by withdrawing more balance from one asset than you actually have in the Dolomite protocol, further utilizing your collateral. This is also evident since BalanceCheckFlag is hardcoded to NONE which means that no checks will be performed, and withdrawing more than you have is possible and the system design allows it.

- The Dolomite connector never implements any health factor OR balance checks allowing for this state to be achieved without actually going through the borrow mechanisms. The Account Status struct on Dolomite is never queried thus there's no way to know if the account is in a borrowing/liquidatable state, etc.

I respectfully must disagree that this is not of a Medium severity, as a very important functionality of the connectors - their ability to repay their debt - would be DOSed unnecessarily in turbulent market conditions, when keeping positions healthy is of detrimental importance.
Given that the repayment of debt positions would not be possible under certain market conditions and that NOYA's positions would be at risk of liquidation, I believe this issue classifies for medium severity.
Also an issue with a very similar end effect has been deemed valid in the past.

patch.explanation: When calculating the TVL of a position held by the AerodromeConnector, make sure to include the accumulated rewards by calling Gauge::rewards(addressOfTheConnector) to get the amount of unclaimed rewards. Determine the value of the rewards by calling getValue for the reward token and add the value to the returned TVL of the position.

attack_path.action: The calculated TVL of a vault is the basis to determine how much value a user gets when withdrawing shares from the vault.
if a user redeems 10% of all vault shares he will get 10% of the calculated TVL.

Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, because the unclaimed rewards are not included in the calculation, any user who withdraws from the vault will receive less value for his shares than he should be receiving.

The calculated TVL is also used to determine how many shares a user gets when depositing to the vault by multiplying the value the user wants to supply with the outstanding shares and dividing it by the calculated TVL.
Since the calculated TVL is lower than the actual TVL, users depositing to the vault will get more share minted to them than they should be getting.

patch.explanation: Considder adding the variable checkHF to the executeCommands function. When checking the method selector in executeCommands, check if the selector is the selector for decreaseDebt. At the end of the function call CreditManagerV3.calcDebtAndCollateral and use the returned values for totalDebtUSD and twvUSD to calculate the new HF of the account (twvUSD /totalDebtUSD). If the result is smaller than the mHF make the function revert.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @gzeon-c4, 
I am wondering why this issue, which was confirmed by @HadiEsna as a med, is downgraded to a QA because of a missing POC. As stated, and linked to in the description, the return values from the SNX protocol have always 18 decimals. If these values are used to calculate the TVL for tokens with less than 18 decimals (e.g USDC or USDT) the value will be off by miles and will allow users to withdraw much more than they should get. And since the return values are only used for calculating and not displaying, this can not be a display issue. 
Would be great if you could reconsider the downgrade.

Thanks!

@gzeon-c4 
 My reasoning for insufficient quality:

 Verdict: Fault in out-of-scope library, impact in in-scope contract, to reward or not to reward
 We would like to clarify the situation where an in-scope contract composes/inherits with an OOS contract, and the root cause exists in the OOS contract. In such cases, the finding is to be treated as OOS, while exceptional scenarios are at the discretion of the judge.

 

Even if valid, the root cause is definitely in the OOS contract (even if it affects in-scope contracts), and the mitigation must be made in the OOS contract.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @gzeon-c4, thank you for judging this contest. Must have been a grind to go through so many submissions that fast.
About the issue in hand, respectfully, I'm afraid I have to disagree with this resolution.
The point of the issue is that the minimumHealthFactor (mHF) is used differently in the SiloConnector and therefore increasing it, which would normally make the position healthier will make the position less healthy.

In all other connectors the mHF is set to 15e17. With a precision of 1e18 this mean that the ration collateralValue/borrowValue should be at least 150%. In the constructor of the SiloConnector the initial MINIMUMHEALTHFACTOR and therefore the lowest value the mHF can be set to is set to 5e17. This represents 50% on a 1e18 scale. 
This deviation from the norm is because in the SiloConnector the mHF is used to determine how may % of the max amount I can borrow against my collateral I should be able to borrow. So e.g. if the max amount I can borrow against my collateral is 100 USD, a mHF of 5e17 allows me to borrow 50USD (more detailed description in the issue above). 

Normally if I increase the mHF I would expect that I can borrow less to keep my position further away from liquidation. In the Silo connector this is the opposite. If I increase the mHF to let’s say 1e18, I can borrow more (100% of the max borrow amount) which makes my position less healthy and closer to liquidation. And since you can not decrease the mHF below the set MINIMUMHEALTHFACTOR because trying so will revert, this breaks a key functionality of the customizable connector. Namely the ability to increase the buffer between the amount one can borrow and the liquidation threshold of the protocol one interacts with. Therefore, this should be a valid issue. 

Would be great if you could take a second look.

For example the max % borrowable for Eth collateral is 60% meaning that for each 1000 USD value of Eth provided as collateral a user can borrow a maxBorrowAmound of 600 USD.

attack_sequence: Sets the fallback handler address of the safe to be the address of the token he rented which he wants to hijack, let's say it's an ERC721 token.
Sends a `transferFrom(from, to, tokenId)` call to the gnosis safe contract while supplying the following parameters:
`from` -> the address of the rental safe holding the token.
`to` -> the address of the attacker himself.
`tokenId` -> the ID of the token he wants to hijack.

Since it's the gnosis rental safe talking to the the rented token contract, and since the rental safe is the owner of the NFT, the ERC721 rented token contract will happily make the transfer and send the token to the attacker.
Token is hijacked, and the lender of the token won't be able to get it back or get the funds he's supposed to receive from the rental process.
You'll need to add the following two files to the test/ folder:
`SetupExploit.sol` -> Sets up everything from seaport, gnosis, reNFT contracts
`Exploit.sol` -> The actual exploit PoC which relies on `SetupExploit.sol` as a base.

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xStalin-eth
submission_issue_comments.body:
@0xA5DF 

It has nothing to do with #593. The main issue of #593 is that there is missing validation on the setFallbackHandler function of the guard, allowing an attacker to set the fallback handler address to be the address of token he wants to rent and hijack it. Meanwhile this one's main issue is that tokens are transferred prior to being registered allowing reentrancy and therefore, the hijacking of tokens.

The impact of both bugs is even different. #593 allows an attacker to hijack any rented ERC721 & ERC1155 while this one allows for the hijacking of ERC1155 only.

Fallback handling setting itself is a crucial feature as it extends the capability of the gnosis safe. For example, If you want to take a uniswap flash loan, then you'll need to implement a custom fallback handler which implements the uniswapV3SwapCallback() function.

In short, the main issue is that #593 doesn't validate the address supplied to setFallbackHandler as it should, and the main issue with this reported bug is that tokens are transferred directly to the rental safe prior to being registered.

Both bugs have different impact, root cause and fix.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @xuwinnie 

 I don't see how the fallback handler can make such instruction

So there are two ways for this:

1. The first way: The attacker can set the custom fallback handler contract to be an owner of the safe, therefore it would be allowed to communicate with the safe and transfer the tokens out of it bypassing the guard (since the rental would not be registered at this point)

2. The second way (ones implemented in the PoC): the attacker (owner of the safe) signs a gnosis safe TX which would transfer the tokens out of it. And then the attacker supplies that signature and TX calldata to the custom fallback handler and then the custom fallback handler will call the gnosis safe and provide it with the TX calldata and the signature. Gnosis will allow this normally since the signature provided is ones signed by the owner of the safe (attacker), and will execute the TX.

 since this the report does not mention how to bypass the guard

The report clearly discusses how the guard is bypassed, please read the report carefully before commenting.

 7. When the onERC1155Receive() callback is executed in the custom fallback handler contract, the fallback handler will instruct gnosis to move the ERC1155 token rented to the attacker's address. submission_issue_comments.author: 0xStalin-eth
submission_issue_comments.body:
@0xA5DF 

It has nothing to do with #593. The main issue of #593 is that there is missing validation on the setFallbackHandler function of the guard, allowing an attacker to set the fallback handler address to be the address of token he wants to rent and hijack it. Meanwhile this one's main issue is that tokens are transferred prior to being registered allowing reentrancy and therefore, the hijacking of tokens.

The impact of both bugs is even different. #593 allows an attacker to hijack any rented ERC721 & ERC1155 while this one allows for the hijacking of ERC1155 only.

Fallback handling setting itself is a crucial feature as it extends the capability of the gnosis safe. For example, If you want to take a uniswap flash loan, then you'll need to implement a custom fallback handler which implements the uniswapV3SwapCallback() function.

In short, the main issue is that #593 doesn't validate the address supplied to setFallbackHandler as it should, and the main issue with this reported bug is that tokens are transferred directly to the rental safe prior to being registered.

Both bugs have different impact, root cause and fix.

If I miss sth please correct me, thanks!

the fallback can be set by the safe owner so basically it can execute any logic the user wants it to, and the call to fallback will not be checked by the guard().

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xStalin-eth
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @xuwinnie 

 I don't see how the fallback handler can make such instruction

So there are two ways for this:

1. The first way: The attacker can set the custom fallback handler contract to be an owner of the safe, therefore it would be allowed to communicate with the safe and transfer the tokens out of it bypassing the guard (since the rental would not be registered at this point)

2. The second way (ones implemented in the PoC): the attacker (owner of the safe) signs a gnosis safe TX which would transfer the tokens out of it. And then the attacker supplies that signature and TX calldata to the custom fallback handler and then the custom fallback handler will call the gnosis safe and provide it with the TX calldata and the signature. Gnosis will allow this normally since the signature provided is ones signed by the owner of the safe (attacker), and will execute the TX.

 since this the report does not mention how to bypass the guard

The report clearly discusses how the guard is bypassed, please read the report carefully before commenting. 

From the report:
 7. When the onERC1155Receive() callback is executed in the custom fallback handler contract, the fallback handler will instruct gnosis to move the ERC1155 token rented to the attacker's address. The gnosis guard will be disarmed and will allow the transferral to occur normally because it isn't aware of the rental at this point.

----

@ding99ya Exactly this.

Hey @0xean I'd recommend to consider this bug report as valid.

Further regarding the rules around OOS contracts, the Supreme Court verdicts states that:
 We would like to clarify the situation where an in-scope contract composes/inherits with an OOS contract, and the root cause exists in the OOS contract. In such cases, the finding is to be treated as OOS, while exceptional scenarios are at the discretion of the judge.

This statement speaks about OOS "contracts" not "files". The libraries/RentalConstants.sol file which you are considering as contract is not actually a contract or library. It is just a solidity file where protocol specific constants are saved. It should be obvious that if a contract uses XYZ variable then the actual value of that XYZ variable should be in audit scope.

I believe this case to be a grey area/exception hence the discretion of the judge should come into play.

patch.explanation: Mitigation review status: Mitigation Confirmed. Reviewer reports: EV_om, sin1st3r__, juancito

attack_sequence: Two orders are created (these will act as our victim orders). One will be for an ERC721 token and the other will be for an ERC1155 token.
Our `attackerContract` is created.

`x` amount of wei (for an arbitrary ERC20) is sent to our `attackerContract`. `x == num_of_victim_orders`. These funds will be used when the `attackerContract` programatically creates the malicious rental orders (our `attackerContract` will behave as `lender` and `renter`).
A `safe wallet` is created (`attacker safe`) and our `attackerContract` is initialized as an owner for that safe.
A generic signature is obtained via a `OrderMetadata` struct from one of the target orders that were initially created (in practice the order used can be any order).

This same process is done for the `AdvancedOrder` structs that are required for the fulfillment transaction (i.e. `Seaport::matchAdvancedOrders`). The `AdvancedOrder` structs are then stored in the `attackerContract` for later use.

The `Fulfillment` struct (required during the `Seaport::matchAdvancedOrders` function call) is pre-constructed. This struct willl remain the same for all of our order creations. This struct is also stored in the `attackerContract` for later use.
Using the `items` field of the `victim RentalOrder`, we will create our malicious `RentalOrder`.

The `attackerContract` will initiate a call to `stopRent` and pass in our malicious `RentalOrder`. However, we will first set `RentalOrder.rentalWallet` equal to the `rentalWallet` of our victim `RentalOrder` (the `safe wallet` that we will be stealing the NFT from).

Steps 9 - 11 will be performed for multiple victim `RentalOrders` by looping over the orders and computing the necessary malicious `RentalOrders`. This time, instead of the `attackerContract` initiating a call to `stopRent`, a call to `stopRentBatch` will be initiated and an array of the malicious `RentalOrders` will be supplied.
The resulting state will be validated: `attacker safe` is now the owner of all the stolen NFTs and the victim `RentalOrders` can no longer be stopped (even after their expiration).
poc.expected_impact: Combined, the above vulnerabilities allow the theft and freezing of any and/or all NFTs currently being rented out (active or expired, as long as the rental has not been stopped).

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xJCN
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @0xean,

I believe this report should be labeled as high severity since it demonstrates a way for an attacker to directly steal and freeze user assets. In addition, I would like to bring some details to your attention that may have been overlooked. My report discusses an exploit path which leverages 3 distinct bugs. Below I will list the primary reports that have been labeled for each of these bugs:

- Primary for bug #1 (see description in my report): 466
 - This issue does not demonstrate a direct theft of assets as the attacker only gains temporary ownership of the NFT during the callback. After the transaction execution, the NFT remains in the custody of the victim' safe wallet and the rental payment for the victim's rental order is unaffected. However, I have shown in my report that by combining multiple bugs (including the one mentioned in report 446), an attacker can directly steal any rented NFT (ERC721/ERC1155) and consequently freeze the rental payments for the affected rental order in the escrow contract. 

- Note regarding bug #2 (see description in my report):
 - You are able to observe all reports which have also identified this root cause under this previously primary submission: 179. Note that these submissions have been inaccurately labeled as dups for 239. Exploitation for bug #2 is not dependent on bug #3 (see details from my report). As described in my report, the root cause for these two bugs are distinct and not dependent on eachother. Therefore, I think It would be more appropriate to revert to the initial evaluation of 179 (label 179 as primary for this distinct root cause). 

- Primary for bug #3 (see description in my report): 239
 - Issue 239 does not demonstrate how to leverage this bug in order to directly steal assets. In my report I have demonstrated how to leverage this bug, in combination with the other bugs mentioned above, to directly steal assets from users. Note that some duplicates of this issue (583, 559, 464, 454, 385, 259, 241, 217, 200, 122, 67, 25) have demonstrated how to leverage only this bug in order to only steal ERC1155 tokens (Some requirements for these issues: 1. The affected order must contain an ERC1155 token. 2. The attacker must have an active rental order for the same ERC1155 token). Note that I have also discussed this exploit in my report in detail (see Further description and lesser impacts of bug #3 section in my report) and have also provided an additional POC for this exploit (see gist in report). However, since the main exploit path in my report demonstrates how to steal any and multiple rented NFTs at once (ERC721/ERC1155), without the need for the attacker to initially own any NFTs and create an active rental, I believe the main exploit path from my report can be considered of greater impact than the exploit demonstrated in the above issues (also discussed in my report).

Based on the information above, I would like to ask you to please re-evaluate this report. I believe this report can potentially be handled in one of two ways: 
1. Considering the fact that this report demonstrates the Identification and demonstration of the maximum achievable impact of the root cause (for each root cause identified above) by combining the 3 root causes, this report can be labeled as primary and all other reports mentioned above (including their duplicates) can be considered duplicates of this report (severity will not be the same between all duplicates since most fail to demonstrate high severity impacts). 
2. Since this report demonstrates a unique impact via the combination of the 3 distinct root causes listed above, this report can be considered as a primary with no duplicates (stand alone report). 

I appreciate you taking the time to read my comment.

Edit: Tagging the sponsor in case they would like to observe, confirm the POC provided in my report. 

@Alec1017

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @0xean, 

Thank you for taking the time to address the issues in my previous comments. 

I believe all duplicates of this report show a lesser impact than what this report demonstrates. For this reason, I believe each duplicate should receive some amount of partial credit since they do not fulfill the requisites for a full mark. Here are the requisites for a full mark as defined in the supreme-court-decisions-fall-2023:

 The requisites of a full mark report are:
 - Identification and demonstration of the root cause
 - Identification and demonstration of the maximum achievable impact of the root cause

This report demonstrates how an attacker can steal any, and multiple, NFTs (ERC721 & ERC1155) at once. Additionally, the attacker does not need to own any NFTs prior or create any rental orders themself prior to the exploit (rental orders are created during the exploit and immediately stopped in the same tx). For reference, the current duplicates (the ones that do not have 25% partial credit) demonstrate how an attacker can only steal ERC1155 tokens. Moreover, for this lesser impact the attacker must first own an ERC1155 of the same tokenId as the victim and must also create a rental order prior to the exploit. 

Based on the information above, I believe the duplicates of this report fail to fulfill the second requisite for a full mark: Identification and demonstration of the maximum achievable impact of the root cause.

Thank you for taking the time to read my additional comment.

The maximum impact this report demonstrates is that actively rented NFTs can be stolen and therefore affected rentals are freezed, and this impact is actually already demonstrated in a lot of the duplicates of this issue.

#385 (freeze rentals)"Missing rentalWallet in signature leads to bricked ERC1155 rentals and stuck assets" 

 I believe all duplicates of this report show a lesser impact than what this report demonstrates.

Therefore, I don't think this is true.

attack_sequence: Carol signs a normal `PAY` rental order with an NFT + ERC20 tokens as an offer
Carol signs the malicious `PAYEE` counterpart order setting the recipient as her address (instead of the Safe for the NFT, and the ESCRW for the ERC20 tokens)
Carol matches those orders via the forked SeaPort
SeaPort calculates the `totalExecutions`, and since all offers and considerations are from the same address, there are no executions, as there will be no transfers
Both the `PAY` & `PAYEE` ordered are fulfilled and call `Create::validateOrder()`
No recipient checks are performed, since there are no executions

The `STORE` storage [will add the new rental](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Create.sol#L595) for Carol, while [increasing the deposit amount in the Escrow](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Create.sol#L601)
SeaPort ends the order matching and fulfillment without performing any transfer
The rent can be stopped and it will drain the Escrow contract of any token + amount specified in the fake rent

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xStalin-eth
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @0xean 

I believe this report should be de-duplicated from #302 and #323 and they should be marked as invalid (#323 however, discusses two issues, one valid (burnable bug), one invalid (permit)). 

While they are saying that there is an issue with permit(), they are providing a completely wrong root cause, wrong explanation of the issue and of how permit() itself works, and they provide zero written or coded PoC for this particular issue. This bug is very different in it's nature from the burnable tokens bug.

What both reports are saying is that the guard doesn't protect against the permit() function selector, allowing a rental safe owner (attacker) to execute a call to permit() and hijack the tokens. 
From #302 
 Guard doesn't block ERC721Permit's permit function. A renter can execute a transaction on the safe that calls this function in which they approve themselves and then steal the NFT. This is possible by calling rentalSafe.executeTransaction() with a CALL operation.


In reality, there is absolutely no need for an attacker to call permit() through the rental safe to exploit this. permit() itself doesn't care about who is the msg.sender, it only cares about the signature you provide it. Therefore, adding permit() to the guard's list of blacklisted function selectors is totally useless.

Let me simplify how permit() itself works: If, for example, Jack owns the NFT ID 6 and he signs a message saying "I, Jack, approve Sean to spend the NFT of ID 6 which I own", and then jack gave this signature to anybody. If anybody called permit() and gave it this signature, it'll will simply check the owner of the NFT and check if it's indeed the owner (Jack) who signed this message, then it will make the approval and let Sean spend the NFT. It doesn't matter who made the call to permit() as I stated.

How this would be exploited would be as following (explained previously in report):
1. The attacker (EOA) rents a permittable NFT on his rental safe
2. The attacker (EOA) signs a digest approving himself (EOA addr or another contract he owns) to spend the token.
3. The attacker, from any contract/EOA account other than the rental safe, sends a call to permit() and supply it with the signature
4. Permit will check who the owner of the NFT is, in this case it's the attacker's rental safe (smart contract), so it'll reach out to the rental safe and ask it if the signature provided is valid (EIP-1271)
5. Gnosis will verify that the signature is indeed signed by the owner of the safe, so it'll return the magic 4 bytes
6. Permit will conduct the approval

A full-fledged coded PoC is attached in the report.

To conclude, as I stated earlier, this bug can never be fixed by just adding permit() to the guard's list of blacklisted function selectors (their suggested fix). The guard itself can never protect against this. One effective way to fix it is included in this report, it'll involve making a small modification to the Gnosis safe contracts.

 I do think that its a pre-condition for this attack and therefore might be better classified as M severity.

Regarding severity, I personally think this should be a High if we consider the burnable tokens bug to be a Med. Simply because this bug allows for the hijacking of the NFT completely. 
That would be a higher impact than being able to make stopRent() revert while not being able to remove NFT from the safe and the attacker will get to own and use the NFT forever, unlike the burnable bug where it's gone if he burns it.

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xStalin-eth
submission_issue_comments.body:
Hey @0xean 

I believe this report should be de-duplicated from #302 and #323 and they should be marked as invalid (#323 however, discusses two issues, one valid (burnable bug), one invalid (permit)). 

While they are saying that there is an issue with permit(), they are providing a completely wrong root cause, wrong explanation of the issue and of how permit() itself works, and they provide zero written or coded PoC for this particular issue. This bug is very different in it's nature from the burnable tokens bug.

What both reports are saying is that the guard doesn't protect against the permit() function selector, allowing a rental safe owner (attacker) to execute a call to permit() and hijack the tokens. 
From #302 
 Guard doesn't block ERC721Permit's permit function. A renter can execute a transaction on the safe that calls this function in which they approve themselves and then steal the NFT. This is possible by calling rentalSafe.executeTransaction() with a CALL operation.


In reality, there is absolutely no need for an attacker to call permit() through the rental safe to exploit this. permit() itself doesn't care about who is the msg.sender, it only cares about the signature you provide it. Therefore, adding permit() to the guard's list of blacklisted function selectors is totally useless.

Let me simplify how permit() itself works: If, for example, Jack owns the NFT ID 6 and he signs a message saying "I, Jack, approve Sean to spend the NFT of ID 6 which I own", and then jack gave this signature to anybody. If anybody called permit() and gave it this signature, it'll will simply check the owner of the NFT and check if it's indeed the owner (Jack) who signed this message, then it will make the approval and let Sean spend the NFT. It doesn't matter who made the call to permit() as I stated.

How this would be exploited would be as following (explained previously in report):
1. The attacker (EOA) rents a permittable NFT on his rental safe
2. The attacker (EOA) signs a digest approving himself (EOA addr or another contract he owns) to spend the token.
3. The attacker, from any contract/EOA account other than the rental safe, sends a call to permit() and supply it with the signature
4. Permit will check who the owner of the NFT is, in this case it's the attacker's rental safe (smart contract), so it'll reach out to the rental safe and ask it if the signature provided is valid (EIP-1271)
5. Gnosis will verify that the signature is indeed signed by the owner of the safe, so it'll return the magic 4 bytes
6. Permit will conduct the approval

A full-fledged coded PoC is attached in the report.

To conclude, as I stated earlier, this bug can never be fixed by just adding permit() to the guard's list of blacklisted function selectors (their suggested fix). The guard itself can never protect against this. One effective way to fix it is included in this report, it'll involve making a small modification to the Gnosis safe contracts.

 I do think that its a pre-condition for this attack and therefore might be better classified as M severity.

Regarding severity, I personally think this should be a High if we consider the burnable tokens bug to be a Med. Simply because this bug allows for the hijacking of the NFT completely. 
That would be a higher impact than being able to make stopRent() revert while not being able to remove NFT from the safe and the attacker will get to own and use the NFT forever, unlike the burnable bug where it's gone if he burns it.

submission_issue_comments.author: udsene
submission_issue_comments.body:
@0xean,

Thank you very much for judging this contest. This issue is marked as a duplicate of issue #462. This issue describes a different vulnerability that could arise as a result of using ERC777 tokens for a PAY order. 

The issue here is that once the PAY order is fulfilled the renter can opt not use the NFT to play a game or for any other reason thus the lender will not get any benefit from lending out his NFT. Hence the lender can decide to cancel the PAY order immediately by calling the stopRent method in stop policy. This will call the settlePayment in escrow module

But the malicious renter can use the tokensReceived hook to revert the transaction thus locking the lender's asset permanently since it is not possible for the lender to cancel the rent of the PAY order. The renter is not losing anything here since he did not invest his time to play using the NFT and he doesn't deserve any payment as a result.

The documentation of the contest did not mention that the ERC777 is out of scope and this vulnerability shows how the use of ERC777 hooks can prompt loss of funds (ERC721 NFT) to the lender when using a PAY order.

Hence i think the impact of this issue deserves a medium severity. 

Thank You

judge_and_sponsor_quotes.quote:
Tested out the PoC. I believe it to be a valid PoC that correctly demonstrates the concept.

However, the asset cannot be "stolen" since it must be given back to the rental safe by the time the "flash steal" ends.

So, I wouldnt say it results in direct loss of funds, or even temporary freezing of funds.

I will say that this does allow the attacker to interact with the asset in any way they see fit, which directly bypasses restrictions that the lender enables via hook contracts. I could see an example where a flash stolen NFT is used with a function selector on a contract to interact with some on-chain game, which the lender may have explicitly wanted to forbid. 

But I'll leave the final decision on the severity to the judges on this.

The PR [here](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/pull/13) - Checks if a rental order exists right away when stopping a rental. Prevents stopping of an order that doesn't exist, only to create it during a callback in the `stopRent()` execution flow.

patch.explanation:
Provide a method for users to migrate old rentals to the upgraded contracts, such as a migrate() function, executable by them or the protocol.
Another way is to provide a way to stop all rentals before the upgrade, in order to start with a fresh new module, or allow users to stop rentals from old modules.
Alec1017 (reNFT) acknowledged, but disagreed with severity and commented:
 This is intended behavior. Upgrading modules is seen as an extremely rare thing, which will only be done in the absense of active rentals.
 
 Would probably be more appropriate for this to be QA.
0xean (Judge) commented:
 @Alec1017 - How would this state be achieved? If the protocol is seeing broad adoption it seems likely that there are essentially always going to be outstanding rentals with no clear ability to recall them all.
Alec1017 (reNFT) commented:
 Our co-signing technique allows us to stop signing off on allowing new rentals, so if we wanted to upgrade everything, we would stop co-signing on orders that use the old contracts and wait for all active orders to expire.
 
 Of course, this only works when a max rent duration is introduced, which is a planned mitigation for this audit.
0xean (Judge) commented:
 Thanks. I think M is the correct severity since the code as audited doesn't practically allow for this functionality to work without major implications. Even with a max duration, essentially pausing the protocol for that long is a DOS and probably means M is correct.
Alec1017 (reNFT) commented:
 Hey there, I dont think I was very clear about the point of upgrading in this manner. Upgrading via the kernel is not meant to be the "normal" way a storage contract is upgraded, this is why they're proxies as well.
 
 Our protocol is modular, which allows the deployment of multiple versions of the same contracts. In the future, you could imagine multiple iterations of our protocol being introduced, which can be rolled in and out simultaneously. We can choose to deprecate one storage module by only allowing people to stop rentals via the situation i described above, and also allow them to initiate rentals with newer versions.
 
 Hopefully this is helpful context!

submission_issue_comments.author: 0xStalin-eth
submission_issue_comments.body:
Marking as QA is probably more appropriate as the mitigation can potentially lead to as many problems as it solves.

@0xean I agree and I believe this one should be a QA at max since the burnable ERC721/1155 bug (much more impactful) is judged as med severity, and here is why:
1. This pausable token will be claimable as soon as they are unpaused by admin, whereas burnable tokens where they are gone forever and will never be reclaimable.
2. The pausable token would only be pausable by an admin, whereas burnable tokens can be burned by anyone as long as he/she owns the NFT they are trying to burn.
3. I believe such pausable tokens are rarer than tokens implementing the burn functionality.
4. And that's the reason you already stated, there really isn't a way to mitigate this just like there isn't a way to mitigate ERC721/1155 tokens that deviate from the standard ERC in addition to deviating from the popular and heavily used extensions (burnable, permit, etc)

submission_issue_comments.author: said017
submission_issue_comments.body:
1. The idea is that a paused token can cause earnings to keep growing. That is why the transfer of NFTs and stopRent should be decoupled. This is a best practice of pull-over-push.

2. It has nothing to do with burn functionality and cannot be compared.

3. I provide AxieInfinity as an example, a widely known NFT game in crypto. It is similar to a blacklistable feature for ERC20 tokens. Not all tokens have such functionality, but if it is widely used, it will become something that needs to be always considered. For instance for blacklistable, USDC implements the functionallity, so it is significantly important to consider such tokens.

4. As I provided and mentioned, decoupling the NFT claim and stopRent is a way to do this.

submission_issue_comments.author: said017
submission_issue_comments.body:
I actually have a different issue that is also a duplicate of #323 (#212). This is distinct, it is not something that should or could be managed by the safe checkTransaction, it should be managed via pull-over-push design. It is an ERC721/1155 extension behavior that could lead to a different issue.

By the way, I do not necessarily agree with the term "Non-standard ERC". Just because ERC721/ERC1155 has extension functionality doesn't mean it is not ERC721/ERC1155. In fact, OpenZeppelin (OZ) also provides some ERC721/ERC1155 extension functionality, which is considered aligned with the ERC721/ERC1155 standard :

Consider a scenario where the lender is not satisfied with how the renter utilizes their PAY order's NFTs.
Now, when the lender wants to early stop the rent and calls stopRent, the call will revert, and the earning calculation for the renter will still be growing.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Marking as QA is probably more appropriate as the mitigation can potentially lead to as many problems as it solves.

@0xean I agree and I believe this one should be a QA at max since the burnable ERC721/1155 bug (much more impactful) is judged as med severity, and here is why:
1. This pausable token will be claimable as soon as they are unpaused by admin, whereas burnable tokens where they are gone forever and will never be reclaimable.
2. The pausable token would only be pausable by an admin, whereas burnable tokens can be burned by anyone as long as he/she owns the NFT they are trying to burn.
3. I believe such pausable tokens are rarer than tokens implementing the burn functionality.
4. And that's the reason you already stated, there really isn't a way to mitigate this just like there isn't a way to mitigate ERC721/1155 tokens that deviate from the standard ERC in addition to deviating from the popular and heavily used extensions (burnable, permit, etc)

submission_issue_comments.author: said017
submission_issue_comments.body:
1. The idea is that a paused token can cause earnings to keep growing. That is why the transfer of NFTs and stopRent should be decoupled. This is a best practice of pull-over-push.

2. It has nothing to do with burn functionality and cannot be compared.

3. I provide AxieInfinity as an example, a widely known NFT game in crypto. It is similar to a blacklistable feature for ERC20 tokens. Not all tokens have such functionality, but if it is widely used, it will become something that needs to be always considered. For instance for blacklistable, USDC implements the functionallity, so it is significantly important to consider such tokens.

4. As I provided and mentioned, decoupling the NFT claim and stopRent is a way to do this.

patch.explanation:
I see three ways to mitigate this (however, the third one is incomplete):
 Split stopping the rental and transferring the assets into separate steps, so that after stopping the rental, the lender and the renter have to call separate functions to claim their assets.
 Change Stop.reclaimRentedItems() so that it doesn't revert when the transfer is unsuccessful.
 For ERC721 use ERC721.transferFrom() instead of ERC721.safeTransferFrom() to transfer the NFT back to the lender. I believe it is reasonable to assume that the wallet that was suitable to hold a ERC721 before the rental is still suitable to hold a ERC721 after the rental and the onERC721Received check is not necessary in this case. For ERC1155 this mitigation cannot be used because ERC1155 only has a safeTransferFrom() function that always does the receive check. So this mitigation is incomplete.
Alec1017 (reNFT) confirmed
JCN (Warden) commented:
 Hi @0xean ,
 
 It seems Issue #600 also identifies the same root cause as this issue: A lender can implement a malicious callback to DOS the stop calls. 
 
 However, this issue does not demonstrate a freezing of victim (renter) "owned" assets. In this issue the lender (attacker) is allowing their NFT and rental payment to be frozen in order to grief the victim. However, I would argue that the victim is not impacted in a way that warrants a high severity. Although the victim can not receive the proposed rental payment, they will essentially be able to utilize the rented NFT while the lender is "griefing" them. The renter is only losing "theoretical capital" in this situation (i.e. the rental payment, which was supplied by the attacker), but would be gaining access to the rented NFT for additional time.
 
 Meanwhile, issue #600 has identified how to leverage the root cause in this issue with another bug (safe wallet can't differentiate between non-rented and rented ERC1155 tokens) in order to permanently freeze a victim's ERC1155 tokens in their safe wallet. 
 
 Given the information above, can you please provide the rationale behind labeling this issue (and duplicates) as high severity, while labeling issue #600 (and duplicates) as medium severity? Based on my observations it seems this issue (and duplicates) should be of medium severity. However, if its high severity status is maintained, then I would think that issue #600 (and its duplicates) should be of high severity as well since these issues demonstrate a greater impact. 
 
 I appreciate you taking the time to read my comment. 
0xean (Judge) decreased severity to Medium and commented:
 @0xJCN thanks for the comment. 
 
 I have re-read the impact and better understand this issue as a result. I do not agree that this loss is "theoretical", a withheld payment is not theoretical, however it is temporary if the lender has any intention to ever receive back their NFT and therefore since its temporary and not a complete loss I do think M is more appropriate.

patch.explanation:
I see three ways to mitigate this (however, the third one is incomplete):
 Split stopping the rental and transferring the assets into separate steps, so that after stopping the rental, the lender and the renter have to call separate functions to claim their assets.
 Change Stop.reclaimRentedItems() so that it doesn't revert when the transfer is unsuccessful.
 For ERC721 use ERC721.transferFrom() instead of ERC721.safeTransferFrom() to transfer the NFT back to the lender. I believe it is reasonable to assume that the wallet that was suitable to hold a ERC721 before the rental is still suitable to hold a ERC721 after the rental and the onERC721Received check is not necessary in this case. For ERC1155 this mitigation cannot be used because ERC1155 only has a safeTransferFrom() function that always does the receive check. So this mitigation is incomplete.

submission_issue_comments.body:
Hi @0xean, I agree with @0xJCN here but I believe there are a couple of duplicates in this finding which should be de-duped and for which the impact does qualify as high. The issue is largely the same, but these submissions recognize that it can also be exploited by the renter, in which scenario:
- the attacker loses nothing, as they merely temporarily forgo the payment they would have received for the rental
- the victim (the lender) is unable to recover the rented NFT until the renter allows them to do so

See issue #634 for a more detailed description. #379 and #487 are the only duplicates as far as I can see.

attack_path.action: A user sends out a tx to call Factory.
The attacker sees that and front runs it, calling SafeProxyFactory.

The user can mitigate that by first creating a safe with a different set or order of owners, or a different threshold, and then creating the safe they wished to create (the attacker can still keep front-running those txs though).

attack_prerequisites: attacker can still keep front-running those txs though)
first creating a safe with a different set or order of owners, or a different threshold, and then creating the safe they wished to create (the attacker can still keep
security_reasoning.broken_behavior: Consider the following scenario: A user sends out a tx to call Factory.deployRentalSafe() The attacker sees that and front runs it, calling SafeProxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce() directly with the same parameters The user's tx would revert because the safe already exists The user can mitigate that by first creating a safe with a different set or order of owners, or a different threshold, and then creating the safe they wished to create (the attacker can still keep front-running those txs though). A way to mitigate that (prevent front running) is to deploy a fork of SafeProxyFactory with access control - allowing only the protocol's Factory to create new safes.

0xsomeone (Judge) increased severity to High and commented:
 This and all duplicate exhibits highlight that the GASFORRELAY is a hard-coded value and that the overall gas supplied for a cross-chain call can be controlled by a user.
 
 A severity of high is appropriate given that the cross-chain LayerZero channel will be permanently blocked.
 
 None of the submissions have correctly proposed a solution as a mere adjustment of the GASFORRELAY is insufficient. The DecentBridgeExecutor permits arbitrary calls to be made that can force the transaction to run out-of-gas regardless of the gas limit imposed. This is properly defined in #697.
 
 A valid solution for this problem would be a combination of a minimum enforced at the transaction level and a maximum gas consumed enforced at the executor level, ensuring that the gas remainder after the executor performs the arbitrary call is enough to store the failed message. This can be achieved by performing a subtraction from the gasleft value (hard to implement as it would need to take into account the cost of keccak256 encoding the data payload) or by enforcing a fixed value that should be much less than the minimum imposed on the source chain.
 
 This submission was selected as the best given that it illustrates in-depth knowledge of the LayerZero system states and correctly highlights that a user can also maliciously block the channel.
wkantaros (Decent) acknowledged via duplicate #212, but disagreed with severity and commented:
 This vulnerability is not a concern in Layer Zero v2. Decent designed the contracts expecting to use LZ v2 and have since implemented this upgrade.

Validate/require that the dstGasForCall parameter is greater than nativeFee + zroFee or re-engineer the architecture to make the estimateSendAndCallFee() function a mandatory step of the process.

submission_issue_comments.body:
This and all duplicate exhibits highlight that the GASFORRELAY is a hard-coded value and that the overall gas supplied for a cross-chain call can be controlled by a user.

A severity of high is appropriate given that the cross-chain LayerZero channel will be permanently blocked.

None of the submissions have correctly proposed a solution as a mere adjustment of the GASFORRELAY is insufficient. The DecentBridgeExecutor permits arbitrary calls to be made that can force the transaction to run out-of-gas regardless of the gas limit imposed. This is properly defined in #697.

A valid solution for this problem would be a combination of a minimum enforced at the transaction level and a maximum gas consumed enforced at the executor level, ensuring that the gas remainder after the executor performs the arbitrary call is enough to store the failed message. This can be achieved by performing a subtraction from the gasleft value (hard to implement as it would need to take into account the cost of keccak256 encoding the data payload) or by enforcing a fixed value that should be much less than the minimum imposed on the source chain.

This submission was selected as the best given that it illustrates in-depth knowledge of the LayerZero system states and correctly highlights that a user can also maliciously block the channel.

0xsomeone (Judge) decreased severity to Medium and commented:
 The Warden has demonstrated that it is possible for a Stargate-based cross-chain interaction to fail at the swap level perpetually.
 
 While the StargateComposer::clearCachedSwap function exists to retry the same payload, as the Warden states, a sharp market event (i.e. token launch that leads to an upward trend or market crash that leads to a downward event) can cause the swap to fail.
 
 Theoretically, the tokens can be rescued using a flash-loan if they are substantial, however, this would be very unconventional and not a real mitigation to the issue. The proposed solution by the Warden is adequate.
 
 I believe a severity of Medium is more appropriate as the vulnerability relies on external requirements (i.e. a sharp market event), the maximum impact is the user's own funds, and when users specify slippage (i.e. minimum output) they usually factor in the time it takes for a transaction to execute. Network congestion, market events, and cross-chain relay delays all play a role in whether the vulnerability manifests but present external requirements.
Note: For full discussion, see here.

Wrap the whole StargateBridgeAdapter:receiveFromBridge() call into a try/catch and if it reverts send the transferred tokens back to the user.

attack_sequence: User invokes `StargateBridgeAdapter:bridge()` function as part of the whole flow of calling `UTB:bridgeAndExecute()` function.
He is passing the swapData parameters to the remote chain.
`StargateComposer` first transfers the tokens to the `StargateBridgeAdapter` contract.
After that the `StargateBridgeAdapter:sgReceive()` function is executed.
It then calls `UTB:receiveFromBridge` that tries to execute the swap.
If the swap fails, which can frequently occur due to the fact that the swap data is outdated, most commonly minimum amount out gets outdated.
The whole payload gets stored inside the `StargateComposer` contract, and the tokens are left in the `StargateBridgeAdapter` contract.
As the user can only retry the transaction with the same payload, the tokens will be stuck forever.
An example of StargateComposer contract can be seen on: https://stargateprotocol.gitbook.io/stargate/developers/contract-addresses/mainnet#ethereum

Theoretically, the tokens can be rescued using a flash-loan if they are substantial, however, this would be very unconventional and not a real mitigation to the issue. The proposed solution by the Warden is adequate.
